title: Heat Pump vs Oil, Propane and Baseboard Heat

corrective.reason: Revision limit reached with blockers s16, s19, s20 (selective): Deetjen and RMI oil results are both lifetime costs including equipment; treat them alike (cut both from the running-cost answer, or name the measure for both) and leave no dangling reference.
Same blocker as revision 4 (selective lifetime-cost results): s21 recommendation comes from RMI Providence lifetime results; cut s20 and s21 together so s22 follows s15, per the revision-4 review.

sentences.text: If your house runs on propane, heating oil or electric baseboards, someone has probably told you a heat pump is the easy win.
But does a heat pump always beat each of them on running cost, or does one of them break the rule?
The home-energy marketplace EnergySage puts it flatly: "Heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil, and electric resistance heating almost everywhere."

assertions.text: EnergySage wrote that heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil and electric resistance heating almost everywhere.

quote.text: Heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil, and electric resistance heating almost everywhere.
quote.speaker: EnergySage

sentences.note: 'Home-energy marketplace' describes the source: its page offers quotes from installers (statement context: 'access the lowest prices from installers near you').

sentences.text: Abode Energy Management, in a video on heat pump economics in Massachusetts, says home heating oil is "always also going to be more expensive than a heat pump".

assertions.text: Abode Energy Management said home heating oil is always going to be more expensive than a heat pump.

quote.text: always also going to be more expensive than a heat pump
quote.speaker: Abode Energy Management

sentences.text: Yet The Boston Globe reported that in a winter of cheaper oil, even Massachusetts homeowners switching from oil "could see their energy costs increase by a few hundred dollars over the cold season".

assertions.text: The Boston Globe reported that with oil cheaper that year, even Massachusetts homeowners switching from oil could see energy costs rise by a few hundred dollars over the cold season.

quote.text: could see their energy costs increase by a few hundred dollars over the cold season
quote.speaker: The Boston Globe

sentences.note: Context: 'this year, the cost of oil is lower, meaning even homeowners switching from that source could see...'; Massachusetts is in the title ('will Mass. consumers buy in?').

sentences.text: So who is right? Start with the widest view.

A national study estimated that among homes heating mainly with electricity, fuel oil or propane that already have air conditioning, 95 to 100 percent would see lower bills with a heat pump, depending on its efficiency.

assertions.text: For homes heating primarily with electricity, fuel oil or propane and with central or room AC, the study found 95% to 100% nationally would have positive bill savings, depending on heat pump efficiency.
qualifications: The sentence says 'estimated' and 'would see', and limits it to homes that already have air conditioning; s09 gives the weaker result without AC.

sentences.text: The median saving it estimated was $300 to $650 a year.

assertions.text: For those homes the median bill saving was $300 to $650 per year, depending on efficiency.
qualifications: Same population as s07: homes on those fuels with AC.

sentences.text: Homes on those fuels without air conditioning did worse: only 73 to 86 percent would come out ahead, and most of the homes whose bills went up were in hotter climates, where the new cooling cost more than the heating saved.

assertions.text: Only 73% to 86% of the homes heating with those fuels but without central or room AC would have positive bill savings.
Most of the homes with increased energy bills are those in hotter climates but without existing central or window AC, where increased cooling costs outweigh heating cost savings.

sentences.note: The second clause carries Wilson's own explanation (L401-L406): the losses come mostly from new cooling in hot climates, not from heating.

sentences.text: For comparison, among gas-heated homes with air conditioning, the same study put the median anywhere from a $70 loss to a $380 saving, depending on the heat pump.

assertions.text: For homes heating with natural gas and with AC, median bill savings ranged from -$70 to $380 per year depending on heat pump performance level.
qualifications: Like for like with s07-s08: both groups have AC, both are medians, both vary with heat pump performance.

sentences.text: That was an estimate. What about heat pumps running in real homes?
sentences.note: Points back to s07's 'estimated'; carries no figure.

sentences.text: A study of cold-climate heat pumps found the all-electric systems cut heating costs by 53 percent on average, measured against what electric resistance heaters would have used for the same heat.

assertions.text: For all-electric cold-climate heat pump systems, with an electric resistance heater assumed to meet the same load in the baseline, average cost savings were 53%.
qualifications: The sentence names the baseline the study assumed (electric resistance meeting the same load) and limits the figure to the all-electric systems; it says nothing about oil, which this study did not test.

sentences.note: The 33% figure for flex-fuel systems is left out: its propane baseline is stated outside the cited lines.

sentences.text: An evaluation of ductless mini-split heat pumps found them more cost-effective than electric resistance and propane heat at every energy price and every outdoor temperature it examined.

assertions.text: Compared against electrical resistance and propane heating, ductless mini-split heat pumps proved more cost-effective for all energy prices and all outdoor air temperatures.
qualifications: s14 gives this study's exception for oil in the next breath.

sentences.text: Oil was different: there, the relative price of oil decided the outdoor temperature above which the heat pump won.

assertions.text: For oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determined the temperature above which a mini-split became more cost-effective.
qualifications: This is the oil qualification the audit lists, stated beside the propane and resistance result it limits.

sentences.text: So the evaluators advised oil-heated homes to switch the heat pump off when it got very cold, when the oil system would run cheaper: below 8 degrees Fahrenheit in one year, and below 25 degrees the next, depending on that year's energy prices.

assertions.text: The evaluators recommended that oil-heated homeowners turn off the mini-split in very cold conditions, below 8F in 2015 and below 25F in 2016, when an oil-fired system would operate less expensively, depending on energy prices.
qualifications: The thresholds are tied to their year's prices in the sentence; the passage says they depend on energy prices and cold-temperature performance.

sentences.note: L1196-L1199: 'turn off a DMSHP during very cold outdoor conditions (below 8°F in 2015 and below 25°F in 2016), when an oil-fired system would operate less expensively (depending on energy prices...)'.

sentences.text: And another study found that in regions where homes heat with electricity or fuels other than gas, heating is generally more expensive and the net benefits of a heat pump are higher, though climate and energy prices also play an important role.

assertions.text: In regions where the heating source is electricity or fuels other than natural gas, heating is generally more expensive and the net benefits of heat pumps are higher; climate and energy prices also play an important role.
qualifications: The sentence keeps the study's caveat that climate and energy prices also matter.

sentences.text: Real projects show the same split: across 273 home electrification projects with cost data, some raised annual energy costs, in some cases by as much as $1,000 a year, while the big reductions were most likely in homes with high bills beforehand, such as those heating with propane or fuel oil.

assertions.text: Among 273 electrification projects with cost savings data, some increased post-retrofit energy costs, by as much as $1,000 per year in some cases, while high reductions in annual energy cost were most likely in homes with high pre-retrofit bills, such as those heating with propane or fuel oil.
qualifications: The sentence says 'electrification projects', not heat pumps alone, and 'most likely', the passage's modality.

sentences.text: So does a heat pump always win?
Against propane and electric resistance heat, this evidence says it nearly always does on running cost.

assertions.text: Against propane and electric resistance heating, ductless mini-splits proved more cost-effective at all energy prices and outdoor temperatures, and the all-electric cold-climate systems saved 53% on average against an electric resistance baseline.
qualifications: 'Nearly always' rather than 'always'; the claim is limited to propane and resistance, the two fuels these studies tested.

sentences.note: Points back to s07-s13 in words; reads no figure again.

sentences.text: Against oil, not always: whether it wins depends on the price of oil and how cold it gets.

assertions.text: For oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determines the temperature above which a mini-split is more cost-effective.

sentences.text: What none of this can do is price your own house: the results moved with air conditioning, climate and energy prices.

assertions.text: Fewer oil, propane and electric homes had positive bill savings without AC, and climate and energy prices play an important role in heat pump net benefits.

sentences.note: The limit that applies to the whole answer; points back to s09, s15 and s22 without re-reading figures.

sentences.text: If you heat with propane or baseboards, get installed quotes and set them against what you spend on fuel each winter.
If you heat with oil, ask a different question: at this winter's oil and electricity prices, below what outdoor temperature does your old system run cheaper, and will you keep it for those days?
sentences.note: Advice built on s14-s15 (a price-dependent switch-over temperature); carries no figure.

sentences.text: Check your fuel and your rates before you check the brochure.
